blocks.text: Lines are strokes that can encompass anything in an image. They can be think or thin and curvy or straight. The nature of the line can invoke movement or emphasis.

The use of shapes in an image can invoke certain design principles and emotions. For example, the use of shapes with soft edges can invoke calmness, with the use of shapes with hard edges and corners can invoke a sense of criticalness or urgency. In the above image, the sharp triangles represent an image that is fierce or dangerous.

Space can be used to direct the viewer's attention to a certain item. Filling an image with too many elements could confuse the viewer when trying to navigate the image. In the above image, the use of white and grey space allows the viewer to focus on the individual walking through the art gallery.

Colour can be used to provoke emotions in the viewer. The use of cool colours for example can invoke calmness, the use of warm colours can be used to invoke excitement and the use of dark colours can be used to invoke danger or urgency. In the above image, the use of light warm colours in the oranges and pineapple contrasting with the yellow background create a feeling of excitement towards the prospect of summer around the corner.
Texture in the image can be used to provoke emotions, a soft surface can appear inviting and pleasing, while a rough surface can appear dangerous or unapproachable.

Tone is simply the lightness or darkness of an image. A lighter tone can be more pleasant while a darker tone can be more dangerous or fearful. While the above image may just be a simple photo of a crowd, the dark tone invoke a sense of danger and fear in the crowd.

Focuses attention on key points. Achieved through contrast (difference) and proportion (size relationships).
One element stands out as most important.

blocks.text: The design principle that measures the weight of elements on a design. Balance can created through the symmetrical or asymmetrical placement of shapes. Balance can also be created through the even use of negative space. In the above image, the even distribution on colour and shapes helps create balance in the image.

Movement is the flow or the direction of a design. Movement can be created through the repetition of similar sized shapes and through the use of line that allows the reader to track and guide the viewer through the design. In the above image, the repetition of the squares directs the viewer to look towards the centre of the image.

Emphasis is created through size proportion and contrast. Contrast is often shown through the element of colour and can be lowly contrast, use of two similar colours, and highly contrast, the use of two different colours - usually opposites on the colour wheel. Proportion is often shown through the size of shapes, text or thickness of lines. The larger the shape of text, the more important the element is regarded in the design, hence is emphasised amongst the design. In the above image, the colours of the individuals in the bath tub contrast against the yellow backdrop, creating emphasis to direct the viewer's attention to the individuals in the tub.
Unity and harmony often go together and refers to the emotions of completeness in the design. The question you ask yourself when assessing unity and harmony is "Do the elements work together?".

Harmony and unity can be created through the use of a consistent colour scheme (e.g. warm or cool colours) and repetition of similar sized shapes. The use of cool colours in the above image as well as the curvy and soft edges of the water creates unity and harmony, producing calming and soothing effect to the viewer.

lessons.title: Logical and Hierarchical Organisation of Content

blocks.text: Considering the Order of Your Content

Readers of a website will not read all of the content of a page. The order of elements placed on a page should be carefully considered to meet the usability needs of the user as well as the purpose of the business's website.

The upper quartile should contain content that the viewer will be initially exposed to. Not all users navigate throughout the entire contents of a page. Place in the upper quartile the elements you want the reader to immediately notice. Items placed in the upper quartile should relate directly to the purpose of the website. It should include items such as:

items: Business name and logo - readers will remember the business by these details for later reference
Address and phone number - easy access to contact details, disgruntled readers who cannot find contact details easily will give up on contacting the business
Information about promotions or specials - this will immediately spark interest in the business's goods or services
Quick links - increase efficiency by allowing users to click on links to take them to their desired pages

blocks.text: This section will contain information that supports the purpose of the business website and other useful tools. The section could include:

items: Customer testimonials - increases creditability of the website
Email subscription services - allow customers to easily join a mailing list to further promote products
Contact forms
Widget of the business's social media page or latest posts

blocks.text: This section is least likely to be viewed by the reader. Include information that is essential but not necessarily assistive towards the purpose of the business website (e.g. the Privacy Act will not necessarily directly increase online sales). This section could include:

items: Copyright
Privacy Act
Terms of Use
Site Map
Social networking sharing tools
Placing the business name and logo at the top will provide immediate exposure to the reader, hence will make the brand more memorable in the future.

Photo gallery shows a photo roll of featured products (eg sale items), as this will entice the viewer and is directly related to the business's website's purpose of generating online sales, hence placed in the upper quartile of the design.

Customer testimonials, frequently asked questions, currency converters, email subscriptions and contact forms all assist in supporting but is not directly related to the website's purpose of generating online sales, hence is placed in the middle quartile.

Footer Items (Privacy Act, Copyright, Terms and Conditions) are necessary to include but are not directly related to generating online sales, hence are placed in the footer in the lower quartile of the design.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Explain the function of the main components of a computer and how their specifications affect usability.

items: Describe the function of each main component of a computer
Identify the specification used to measure each component
Explain how a specification affects usability for a specific user

blocks.title: Inside the Computer
blocks.caption: Watch each component do its job. Exam answers need to link a component's specification to what the user experiences.

pauseQuestions.question: Name the two input devices shown, and one more input device that is not shown.
pauseQuestions.answer: Keyboard and mouse. Others include a microphone, webcam, touchscreen, scanner or game controller.

pauseQuestions.question: Explain why the SSD's packets arrive first, using the term access time.
pauseQuestions.answer: An SSD uses flash memory with no moving parts, so its access time is almost instant. An HDD must spin the platter and move the read/write head to the right track, which adds delay and lowers read speed.

pauseQuestions.question: Programs are copied from storage into RAM before they run. Why not run them straight from storage?
pauseQuestions.answer: RAM is far faster than storage, so the CPU can fetch instructions quickly. Running from storage would leave the CPU waiting. The trade-off is that RAM is volatile and more expensive per GB.

pauseQuestions.question: Describe what the CPU is doing with each packet it fetches from RAM.
pauseQuestions.answer: It runs the fetch-decode-execute cycle: fetch the instruction from memory, decode it in the control unit, execute it in the ALU, then store the result back in RAM (or a register).

pauseQuestions.question: Which component turns the result into a picture? Name the two output devices shown.
pauseQuestions.answer: The graphics card (GPU) makes the picture. The output devices are the monitor and the speakers.

pauseQuestions.question: A user says their computer is slow when several programs are open. Using this animation, which component would you upgrade first and why?
pauseQuestions.answer: RAM. When RAM is full, data has to be swapped out to storage, which is much slower. More RAM keeps more programs in fast memory. A strong answer links the specification (for example 8 GB to 16 GB) to what the user notices.

rows: Clock speed (GHz), number of cores, cache
More cores and a higher clock speed run demanding software and multiple applications faster. High-performance CPUs use more power, reducing battery life.
Temporarily stores the data and instructions currently in use. Volatile: contents are lost when power is off.
More RAM lets more applications and larger files stay open without the system slowing down.
Stores the startup instructions (firmware, e.g. UEFI) needed to boot the computer. Non-volatile.
Not usually listed on a spec sheet
Allows the device to start and load the operating system.
Stores the operating system, software and files permanently. Non-volatile.
Capacity (GB or TB), type (SSD or HDD), read/write speed (MB/s)
An SSD starts up and opens files much faster than an HDD and is more durable in a portable device. Capacity limits how many files and applications can be stored.
Processes images, video and 3D graphics for the display
A dedicated GPU with more VRAM supports gaming, video editing and 3D rendering. An integrated GPU suits office work and uses less battery.
Main circuit board that connects all components so they can communicate
Determines the ports available (e.g. USB-C, HDMI) and whether the device can be upgraded.
Connects the device to a network
A newer wireless standard gives faster, more reliable connections, especially on busy networks.
Wattage (W) for desktops; battery capacity (Wh) and rated battery life (hours) for portable devices
A larger battery lets a mobile user work a full day without charging.

items.definition: Loses its contents when power is removed (e.g. RAM).
Keeps its contents without power (e.g. ROM, SSD, HDD).

blocks.title: Fetch, Decode, Execute
blocks.caption: Inside the CPU: how the Control Unit, ALU, registers and buses work together on every instruction.

pauseQuestions.question: Name the three buses used during the fetch and what each one carries.
pauseQuestions.answer: The address bus carries the address from the MAR to RAM. The control bus carries the READ signal. The data bus carries the instruction back from RAM to the MDR.

pauseQuestions.question: Why is the instruction copied from the MDR into the CIR before it is decoded?
pauseQuestions.answer: The CIR holds the current instruction while the Control Unit decodes and runs it. That frees the MDR to carry the next piece of data, such as the value from address 4.

pauseQuestions.question: Trace the value 7 from RAM into the accumulator, naming each register it passes through.
pauseQuestions.answer: The address 4 goes into the MAR and out on the address bus. RAM sends 7 back on the data bus into the MDR, and the MDR copies it into the ACC.

pauseQuestions.question: What do the Control Unit and the ALU each do during ADD 5?
pauseQuestions.answer: The Control Unit decodes ADD 5 and directs the data between registers. The ALU performs 7 + 5, and the result, 12, goes back into the accumulator.

pauseQuestions.question: During STORE 6 the address bus and data bus are used together. What does each carry, and which way does the data move?
pauseQuestions.answer: The address bus carries 6 from the MAR to RAM. The data bus carries 12 from the MDR to RAM. The control bus sends WRITE, so this time data moves from the CPU into memory.

pauseQuestions.question: Explain how a quad-core CPU can process more instructions than a single-core CPU at the same clock speed.
pauseQuestions.answer: Each core has its own control unit, ALU and registers and runs its own fetch-decode-execute cycle, so four instruction streams can run at once. This only helps when the software is multi-threaded and can share its work across cores.

blocks.text:

Strong: "16 GB of RAM lets the designer keep Photoshop and Illustrator open with large image files without the system slowing, so she can move between tasks efficiently."

question.text: A real estate agent spends most of the day visiting properties. She uses a laptop to show property photos to clients and complete contracts on site. Explain how two specifications of a laptop affect its usability for the agent.
question.explanation:
Marking key (per specification, x2):
3 marks – explains how the specification affects usability, linked to the agent
2 marks – describes how the specification affects usability
1 mark – identifies a relevant specification

Answers could include:
- Battery life: a rated battery life of 12 hours or more lets the agent work at properties all day without finding a power outlet, so contracts are not delayed
- Weight: a laptop under 1.5 kg is easy to carry between properties and hold while showing clients photos
- Wireless connectivity: built-in 5G or a current Wi-Fi standard lets the agent access listings and submit contracts from any property
- Display: a bright, high-resolution screen shows property photos clearly to clients, even outdoors
- SSD storage: the laptop starts quickly and opens large photo files without delay while clients are waiting

topics.title: Impacts of Technology
topics.description: Intellectual property, copyright and online defamation law in Australia, the Freedom of Information Act, and the advantages, disadvantages and impacts of virtual collaboration and digital convergence trends.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Describe the concept and purpose of intellectual property (IP) in Australia in relation to digital products.

items: Describe the concept of intellectual property
Explain the purpose of IP laws in Australia
Identify the four types of IP with a digital product example of each

blocks.definition: Legal rights that protect the creators of original works, inventions, brands and designs, giving them exclusive rights to use and profit from them.

blocks.text: Patents, trade marks and registered designs are registered with IP Australia. Copyright is automatic and does not need registering.

items: Rewards creators by giving them exclusive rights to profit from their work
Encourages innovation and investment in new digital products
Prevents others copying or using the work without permission
Gives owners grounds for legal action and compensation if their rights are breached
Lets owners license or sell their rights to others

rows: The original expression of an idea: code, text, images, music, video
A new invention or how something works
A brand: name, logo, slogan, sound or colour
The visual appearance of a product: shape, pattern, colour

blocks.text: Explain how copyright protects digital products and when content can be used legally.

items: Describe what copyright does and does not protect

blocks.definition: Automatically protects the original expression of an idea once it is written down or recorded. No registration is needed. Lasts for the life of the creator plus 70 years.

rows: Ideas, e.g. the idea of a to-do list app
Text, images, icons and website content
Names, titles and slogans (protect these with a trade mark)
Facts and data on their own
Works where copyright has expired (public domain)

question.text: State the purpose of Australian copyright laws in relation to the creation of digital products.

question.text: Describe two copyright issues that can arise from the re-transmission and broadcasting of digital media over the internet.
question.explanation:

question.text: A start-up has created a smart water bottle called HydroTrack. It uses a new sensor that measures how much the user drinks, has a distinctive curved shape, and connects to an app. Identify the type of intellectual property that would protect each of the following, and describe why: (a) the sensor (b) the bottle's shape (c) the name HydroTrack.
question.explanation:
Marking key (for each part, x3, 2 marks per part):
1 mark – identifies the correct type of IP
1 mark – describes why it applies to that part of the product

Answers could include:

- (b) Registered design: the curved shape is the product's visual appearance, which a registered design protects
- (c) Trade mark: HydroTrack is the brand name that identifies the business's product to customers

blocks.heading: Key point
blocks.text:
Patents, trade marks and registered designs granted in Australia only protect you in Australia.
To be protected overseas, you must apply in each country.
Exception: copyright is automatic in most countries.

rows: The Berne Convention: work protected in Australia is protected in over 175 member countries, with no registration
Apply in each country. 12-month priority period.
Apply in each country. 6-month priority period.
Apply in each country. 6-month priority period.

blocks.definition: After applying in Australia, you have 12 months (patents) or 6 months (trade marks and designs) to apply in other member countries. Those applications are treated as if they were filed on your Australian date, so no one can register it first. It is not protection. It only holds your place in the queue.

blocks.heading: Exam tip
blocks.text:
Do not say Australian IP "is protected worldwide".
Only copyright is automatic overseas.
Everything else must be registered in each country.

blocks.definition: Gives every person the legal right to access documents held by Australian Government ministers and agencies, unless the document is exempt. It is overseen by the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC).

blocks.title: Why Freedom of Information matters to all Australians

rows: The public can see how government decisions are made and how public money is spent
Agencies know their records can be requested, which encourages careful, lawful decision-making
Access to information lets people take part in debate and hold government to account
People can see, and ask to correct, information the government holds about them (e.g. Centrelink, tax or immigration records)

items: Covered: Australian Government departments, agencies and ministers (e.g. Services Australia, the ATO, Department of Defence)
Not covered: private companies and individuals. Each state and territory has its own FOI law for state agencies such as public schools, hospitals and police.
Documents include paper files and digital records: emails, text messages, databases, spreadsheets, photos and audio or video recordings
Submit the request in writing, usually through the agency's online FOI form or by email
Clearly describe the documents wanted and state that the request is made under the FOI Act
The agency must make a decision within 30 days (this can be extended, e.g. when third parties must be consulted)
Documents are released in full, released in part (with exempt information redacted), or refused
If refused, the applicant can ask for an internal review by the agency, then an Information Commissioner review by the OAIC

blocks.heading: Costs
blocks.text: There is no application fee. There is no charge for accessing your own personal information. Processing charges may apply to other requests (e.g. time spent searching and making a decision).
An agency can refuse access to a document, or part of it, if an exemption applies.

rows: National security, defence and international relations
Details of military cyber security systems
Information that could compromise a police investigation
Confidential legal advice given to an agency
Another person's address or medical details
A company's trade secrets or commercially sensitive pricing
Draft advice and opinions used during policy development

blocks.heading: Public interest test
blocks.text: Some exemptions (e.g. personal privacy, business information, deliberative processes) are conditional. The document must be released unless releasing it would be contrary to the public interest.

- Business information: the contract may include the supplier's pricing or technical methods, and releasing them could harm the company's commercial position
- Personal privacy: emails may include names and contact details of staff or contractors, so these sections are redacted to protect their privacy
- Deliberative processes: draft advice about choosing the supplier may be withheld if releasing it is contrary to the public interest

blocks.text: Online software is any software program that is interacted with and used partially or fully online. Prior to the growth of the internet, software used to be downloaded or provided on discs where they had to be installed. Nowadays, we can access a world of software instantly online without the need for installation.

items: Canva - Online photo editing
Microsoft OneDrive, Word, PowerPoint, Excel etc - Office applications
Evernote - Note taking software
Xero - Accounting Software

items.definition: Online software can be accessed from anywhere with an internet connection, making it easy to use and share across multiple devices. For example, think of your ability to access Google Docs on any device.
Many online software options offer subscription-based pricing models, which can be more cost-effective for users than traditional software licenses.

Online software is often updated automatically, meaning users always have access to the latest features and security updates without needing to manually install anything. You also don't need to wait to install any software upfront.

Online software can allow multiple users to work on the same document or project simultaneously, making it easier for teams to collaborate and work together. Think collaboration on Canva, Word 365 or Google Docs.
Online software is often compatible with a wide range of devices and operating systems, meaning users can use it on the devices they prefer without needing to worry about compatibility issues.
It's all stored on the web, reducing the amount of space needed on a device!

Online software requires a stable internet connection to work effectively. Poor internet connection or service disruptions can result in lost work or inability to access the software. Imagine working in remote or regional areas with limited internet.

Online software stores data on remote servers, which can raise security concerns. Data breaches can result in loss of sensitive data and compromise the privacy of users. With all data stored online, there is a risk a hacker can take all the sensitive information of a user or business. Think about the security risk Xero or MYOB has in protecting their users' data.
Online software typically has limited customization options, meaning users may not be able to tailor the software to their specific needs or preferences.
Online software relies on servers and infrastructure, which can experience downtime due to maintenance, updates, or unexpected issues, resulting in a lack of access to the software.
While online software can be more cost-effective than traditional software licenses, subscription fees can add up over time and may not be sustainable for some users or businesses.

Mainly at the start and at sign-off points
Small projects, or when requirements are unclear or likely to change
Large projects with clear requirements, fixed deadlines and budgets
An app where the client is unsure what the interface should look like
A bank website with set features, a large team and a fixed launch date

blocks.title: What Is User Generated Content and Can It Help Your Business? | The Journey
blocks.caption: In the above video, the GoDaddy team discuss the importance of user generated content and how it can assist a business.

blocks.definition: Any online content created and published voluntarily by users rather than the business or organisation itself.

items: Social Networking: Facebook, Instagram, YouTube, Tik Tok
Review Platforms: Google Reviews, TripAdvisor, Steam
Online Communities and Forums: Reddit, Whirlpool
Collaborative Websites: Wikipedia
Online Marketplaces: Gumtree
Free - The website owner does not have to pay staff to produce content
General feedback is seen as reliable - General user opinions can be viewed as valuable towards feedback and decision making, e.g. checking the rating of a restaurant before deciding where to eat.
Self-policing opportunities - Forums can be monitored by voluntary moderators

Keeps users engaged - Users often participate in discussions with one another, keeping users engaged and increasing the number of returned users. It adds to the engagement of users without any significant work from the business.

blocks.heading: Disadvantages of User Generated Content
blocks.html:
• Bias – Users often hold strong opinions about a topic and often don't contribute a balanced perspective.
  • Lack of reliability and credibility – Anyone can publish content, from a 5-year-old to a University professor, therefore, user generated content has to be taken with a pinch of salt. There's no guarantee that information presented in user generated content is factual, and that is why Wikipedia has a poor reputation and is often avoided in referencing.
  • Online defamation risk – Users can publish false, offensive or inappropriate content, which could pose a legal liability towards the website owner. In February 2016, an online user on TripAdvisor wrote a defaming review of the Gold Coast hotel Paradise Resort. Such comments could negatively impact the business by deterring future guests from staying at the hotel.
  • Confusion over intellectual property – Who owns user generated content? There is often confusion over who owns user generated content and how it can be used.

blocks.heading: Case Study: Business to Pay $215,000 in Penalties for Fake Testimonials
blocks.html:
In 2015, a carpet cleaning franchisor was ordered to pay $215,000 for fake testimonials on the internet.

The Court found that Electrodry posted, and requested that its franchisees post, customer testimonials about the quality of carpet cleaning services when those customers were fabricated and the services had not been provided. These fake reviews were published on websites including Google, True Local and Yelp. The ACCC took Electrodry to court over false and misleading advertising.

Read the full press release by the ACCC here.

rows: Colours, fonts, spacing, layout for mobile and desktop
Drop-down menus, image sliders, checking a form as the user types

rows: Uses tags to describe and structure content. It is not a programming language: it does not perform calculations or make decisions.
Text containing links (hyperlinks) to other pages or resources

A keyword in angle brackets, usually in pairs: an opening tag

and a closing tag

blocks.text: Explain key methods of securing data in digital systems and evaluate their purpose, function, and effectiveness in protecting data from unauthorised access.

Explain how encryption, digital signatures, and digital certificates use public key infrastructure.

blocks.text: A password is a sequence of characters used to verify a user's identity when accessing a system.

items: Unique for each account
Long and memorable (12 or more characters)
Avoid personal information and common words

blocks.text: Security Role: Passwords authenticate users and help prevent unauthorised access.
A firewall is a security system, either software or hardware, that monitors and filters incoming and outgoing data packets based on defined security rules.
Security Role: A firewall acts as a barrier between trusted internal networks and untrusted external sources, such as the internet.
Biometrics use unique physical characteristics to authenticate users. These may include:

items: Fingerprints
Facial recognition
Iris scans
Voice recognition

blocks.text: Security Role: Biometrics provide access control that is highly specific to the individual and difficult to replicate.
Anti-virus software detects, isolates, and removes malicious software (malware) from computing systems.
How it works: The software scans for malware using a frequently updated list of known virus definitions. It protects against:

items: Trojans
Worms
Ransomware
Spyware

blocks.text: Security Role: Reduces the risk of data corruption, loss, or theft by removing threats before they cause damage.
A digital signature is a cryptographic method that verifies the authenticity and integrity of a digital message or document.
Security Role: Confirms that a document has not been changed since it was signed and verifies the sender's identity.
A digital certificate is an electronic document that verifies the ownership of a public key, issued by a trusted Certificate Authority (CA).
Security Role: Supports secure communication between a user's device and a server, commonly used in HTTPS connections.
Encryption converts data into a coded format that cannot be read without the correct decryption key.

items: Symmetric encryption: Uses the same key for both encryption and decryption.

blocks.text: Security Role: Protects data confidentiality during storage or transmission by ensuring only the intended recipient can access the information.

items: Define backup and archive using correct terminology
Compare backup and archive using at least three criteria
Explain two reasons an organisation archives data

items.definition: A copy of current data stored separately so it can be restored if the original is lost, damaged or corrupted.
The long-term storage of data that is no longer in regular use. The data is moved off the live system and kept for future reference or to meet legal requirements.

rows: Retain data long term for reference or compliance
Inactive data no longer in regular use
Stays on the live system (the backup is a copy)
Removed from the live system (the archive is often the only copy)
Periodic, when data becomes inactive (e.g. end of financial year)
Short term; older backups are overwritten
Files or whole systems restored quickly
Specific records searched for and retrieved; slower

Low-cost, high-capacity media: tape, cold cloud storage

Removing inactive data makes live databases smaller, so they run faster and take less time to back up.

Past records stay available for audits, disputes and trend analysis.

question.text: Compare backing up data with archiving data.

blocks.text: Backup techniques in the WACE syllabus fall under three main types:

items: Full
Differential
Incremental

rows: Copies the entire contents of a system to a separate storage location.
Fastest and simplest restore, as everything sits in one backup set
Uses the most storage space; takes the longest to complete
Copies only the files changed since the last backup of any type (full or incremental).
Uses the least storage space; fastest backup to run
Slowest and most complex restore, as it needs the last full backup plus every incremental in sequence
Copies all files changed since the last full backup.
Simpler, faster restore than incremental, as it only needs the last full backup plus the most recent differential
Uses more space than incremental and grows larger each day until the next full backup is run

blocks.text: Time Machine Backup is a default backup application for the Mac operating system. It is known for its simplicity in use and restoring data from a backup.

It works by starting a full backup on first use. This copies all files and contents on the system onto an external device. After the initial full backup is performed, the software checks for any new data every hour and performs an incremental backup of that data. Backups are performed until storage space on the external device is full, in which the oldest data is deleted.

- Presence check: fields such as name and phone number must be completed before the application can be submitted, so the employer can contact every applicant
- Format check: the email address must contain @ and a domain, so an incorrectly typed email is rejected before submission
- Range check: the date of birth must show the applicant is at least 15, the legal minimum working age for the role
- Length check: the cover letter box is limited to 500 words, so applications stay a manageable size

question.text: Explain why a website should use server-side validation as well as client-side validation.
question.explanation:
3 marks – explains why server-side validation is needed as well as client-side
2 marks – describes a difference between client-side and server-side validation
1 mark – makes a relevant statement

Answers could include:
Client-side validation runs in the browser and can be bypassed by disabling JavaScript or editing the page, so invalid or malicious data could still reach the server. Server-side validation checks the data again after submission, where the user cannot change the rules, so only valid data is stored.

blocks.definition: A large, centralised database used to store historical and current data from multiple sources. Typically used by large organisations (e.g. Spotify, Netflix, government agencies). Stores structured data that can be analysed for business decisions and reporting. Not updated in real time – data is often added in batches.

blocks.text: Data Warehouse vs Database – What's the Difference?

items: A database is used for day-to-day transactions (OLTP – Online Transaction Processing).
Fast, simple queries for things like logging in, making purchases, updating records.
Example: When you stream a song or update your profile, a database handles it.
A data warehouse is used for analysis, not transactions (OLAP – Online Analytical Processing).
Handles complex queries to spot trends or patterns over time.
Example: Used by Spotify to analyse what songs are most played in each country.

blocks.heading: In short
blocks.text: Use a database to run the business. Use a data warehouse to understand the business (for a huge organisation).

blocks.definition: A smaller, more focused version of a data warehouse. Usually used by a single department or team within a company (e.g. the marketing team). Contains only the data relevant to that group, which makes it faster and easier to query. Still supports analysis and reporting, but on a smaller scale.

blocks.heading: Further reading
blocks.html: Data mart vs data lake (Airbyte)

items: Refers to storing data online using cloud storage providers such as Google Drive, Microsoft OneDrive, Dropbox, AWS and iCloud.
Accessible from anywhere with an internet connection.
Can be used for both personal and enterprise data.
Supports real-time collaboration, backup, and auto-sync features.
Ideal for students, remote teams, and mobile access to files.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Explain the purpose of data mining and evaluate its benefits and concerns for organisations and individuals.

items: Define data mining using correct terminology
Describe three purposes of data mining with real-world examples
Explain one benefit for an organisation and one concern for individuals

blocks.definition: The process of analysing large amounts of stored data (often in a data warehouse) to discover hidden patterns, trends and relationships. Organisations use these patterns to make predictions and better decisions.

rows: Website and app activity tracked by cookies
Search history and social media activity

blocks.text: Data from many sources is combined in a data warehouse, then mined to build a detailed profile of each customer.

rows: Customers are grouped by behaviour and interests so offers match each group
A supermarket sends personalised discounts through its loyalty app
Past behaviour is used to predict what a user will want next
Netflix suggests shows; Spotify builds a personalised playlist
Finds products that are often bought together
A store places chips next to dips, or an online shop shows "frequently bought together"
Flags transactions that do not match a customer's normal pattern
A bank blocks a card used overseas minutes after a purchase in Perth
Predicts future sales from past trends, seasons and weather
A supermarket orders more ice cream before a heatwave
Finds patterns in patient records linked to health risks
Identifying patients at higher risk of a disease so they can be screened early
Detects unusual activity in system logs and audit trails
An alert when an employee accesses files they do not normally use
Detailed profiles reveal habits, locations and interests that people never chose to share
Permission is usually hidden in long terms and conditions that few people read
Patterns can reveal sensitive information. A US retailer's model predicted a customer's pregnancy from her shopping before she had told her family.
Large data warehouses are valuable targets for hackers, so a breach exposes millions of records
Data may be sold to or shared with other companies the customer has never dealt with
Decisions based on patterns can unfairly disadvantage groups (e.g. higher insurance prices for certain postcodes)

blocks.heading: The law
blocks.text: Under the Privacy Act 1988, organisations must tell people what personal information they collect and why (collection notice), use it only for that purpose or a related one, and keep it secure. Sensitive information (e.g. health, religion) has stronger protection.

question.text: Describe the purpose of data mining.
question.explanation:
2 marks – describes data mining as analysing large amounts of data to find patterns or trends, used to make predictions or decisions
1 mark – makes a relevant statement, e.g. "finding information in data"

question.text: A supermarket chain collects data through its loyalty card program. Explain one benefit of data mining for the supermarket and one concern for its customers.
question.explanation:
Marking key (for the benefit and the concern, x2):
3 marks – explains in detail, linked to the supermarket and its customers
2 marks – describes the benefit or concern
1 mark – states a benefit or concern

Answers could include:
- Benefit: purchase patterns show which products are bought together and when, so the supermarket can send targeted discounts to each customer and stock the right products, increasing sales and reducing waste
- Concern: the supermarket builds a detailed profile of each customer's habits, and may share it with partner companies or expose it in a data breach, even though most customers did not read the terms when joining the program

topics.title: Networks
topics.description: Communication protocols (TCP/IP, HTTP/HTTPS), communication standards (802.3 Ethernet and 802.11x wireless), and network security measures (firewalls, passwords, physical security), applied to designing and justifying a LAN.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Design a LAN for a client and justify the design choices using the client's needs.

items: Draw a labelled LAN diagram that includes every required component
Choose a suitable communication standard (802.3 or 802.11x) for each device
Justify design choices with direct links to the scenario

blocks.text: A small accounting firm has three staff desktops, a file server storing client tax records, and a shared printer. Staff also use laptops and phones as they move around the office. The firm connects to the internet through the NBN.

items.definition: Cloud symbol.
Connects to your ISP.
Connects networks together (i.e. internet and your LAN).
Sits between the router/modem and the switch.
Connects devices on a network.
Wired devices are connected with Ethernet cables. Show the cables with hard lines in a diagram.
Wireless devices connect to the network.
Every device needs a NIC shown or labelled. Every wireless device needs to show it has a wireless NIC.

blocks.text: Justification formula: design choice + characteristic + link to the client's need.

blocks.heading: Example
blocks.text: "The server is connected by 802.3 Cat6 cable (choice), which gives a fast, reliable connection that cannot be intercepted wirelessly (characteristic), so staff can open client tax files quickly and the confidential records stay secure (link)."

question.text: Describe the role of a switch in a LAN.
question.explanation:
2 marks – describes the role: connects the wired devices in a LAN and forwards data only to the device it is addressed to
1 mark – states a relevant point, e.g. "connects computers together"

question.text: A physiotherapy clinic has a reception computer, two treatment-room computers, a server storing patient records and a printer. Physiotherapists use tablets to record notes as they move between rooms. Justify two design choices you would make in the clinic's LAN.
question.explanation:
For each design choice (x2):
1 mark – identifies a suitable design choice
3 marks – justifies the choice with detailed reasons linked to the clinic
2 marks – justifies the choice with limited reasons or links
1 mark – gives one relevant reason
Subtotal 4 marks per choice; total 8 marks.

Answers could include:
- Wireless 802.11x WAP for the tablets: physiotherapists move between treatment rooms, so wireless lets them record notes at each bed without cables, and WPA3 encryption protects patient information sent over the air
- Server wired with 802.3: patient records are opened all day from every room, so a cable gives a fast, reliable connection, and the server cannot be accessed through the wireless signal
- Hardware firewall between the router and switch: patient records are sensitive health information, so the firewall blocks unauthorised access from the internet before it reaches the server

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Explain how TCP/IP enables reliable communication between devices on different networks.

items: Describe the separate roles of TCP and IP
Distinguish between private and public IP addresses
Explain how TCP/IP transfers data between a device and a web server

blocks.definition: The suite of communication protocols (rules) the internet uses to address, route and reliably deliver data between devices on different networks.

blocks.title: Packet Journey
blocks.caption: This is TCP/IP working end to end. IP gets each packet to the right address. TCP numbers the packets, puts them back in order and confirms they arrived.

pauseQuestions.question: What does each packet's header contain, and what is the rest of the packet called?
pauseQuestions.answer: The header holds the source and destination IP addresses, a sequence number and error-checking data. The rest is the payload, the piece of the message.

pauseQuestions.question: How does a switch decide which port to send data out of?
pauseQuestions.answer: It reads the destination MAC address and looks it up in its MAC address table, so data only goes to the device it is meant for (unlike a hub, which sends it to every port).

pauseQuestions.question: What does the router read, and how does it choose where to send each packet next?
pauseQuestions.answer: It reads the destination IP address and checks its routing table to choose the next hop towards that network.

pauseQuestions.question: Which protocol gets each packet to the right address, and why can packets arrive out of order?
pauseQuestions.answer: IP. It routes every packet independently, so packets can take different paths with different delays.

pauseQuestions.question: Which protocol puts the packets back in order, and what does it use to do it?
pauseQuestions.answer: TCP, using the sequence number in each packet's header.

pauseQuestions.question: What is the green packet called, and how does it make TCP reliable?
pauseQuestions.answer: An acknowledgement (ACK). If the sender gets no ACK for a packet within a set time, it retransmits that packet, so no data is lost.

rows: Every packet carries a source and destination IP address. Routers read the destination address and forward each packet across networks towards it. IP does not guarantee packets arrive, or arrive in order.

Sets up a connection before sending. Breaks data into numbered segments, checks each for errors, and requires the receiver to acknowledge them. Lost or damaged packets are re-sent, and the data is reassembled in the correct order.

blocks.heading: Analogy
blocks.text: IP is the address on each envelope, so the postal network knows where to send it. TCP numbers the pages, checks every page arrived, and asks for any missing page to be sent again.

blocks.heading: Common error: who assigns IP addresses?
blocks.text: IP does not assign addresses. IP defines the address format and uses addresses to route packets. Addresses are assigned by DHCP (dynamic host configuration protocol), usually run by the router on a LAN. The ISP assigns the network's public IP address.

rows: Identifies a device within a local network (LAN). Not reachable directly from the internet. Assigned by the router using DHCP.
192.168.1.5 given to a laptop on a home network
Identifies the whole network on the internet so external servers can send data back. Assigned by the ISP.
203.45.67.89 given to a home or school router

blocks.text: The router uses NAT (network address translation) so many devices with private addresses can share one public address.

rows: About 4.3 billion addresses, which have run out
Enough addresses for every connected device, including IoT devices

blocks.text: How TCP/IP delivers a web page

items: The smartphone has a private IP address from the router (DHCP) and reaches the internet through the router's public IP address
TCP sets up a connection with the web server
The request is broken into numbered packets, each addressed with the server's IP address
IP routes each packet through routers across the internet. Packets may take different paths
TCP on the server checks every packet arrived, requests any missing ones, and reassembles them in order
The server sends the web page back using the same process in reverse

question.text: Distinguish between a private IP address and a public IP address.
question.explanation:
1 mark – private IP address identifies a device within a local network and is not directly reachable from the internet
1 mark – public IP address identifies a network on the internet and is assigned by the ISP

question.text: A student streams a lecture recording from a university web server. Explain how TCP ensures the recording arrives complete and in the correct order.
question.explanation:
3 marks – explains how TCP ensures complete, ordered delivery, linked to the scenario
2 marks – describes how TCP ensures reliable delivery
1 mark – states that TCP ensures reliable delivery

Answers could include:
- TCP breaks the recording into numbered segments. The student's device acknowledges each segment received; any lost or damaged segments are re-sent by the server, and the sequence numbers are used to reassemble the recording in the correct order so it plays without gaps

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Compare the Ethernet (802.3) and wireless (802.11x) communication standards and justify their use in a LAN.

items: Distinguish between a communication standard and a communication protocol
Describe the key characteristics of 802.3 and 802.11x
Justify the choice of communication standard for a specific scenario

items.definition: An agreed specification, set by the IEEE, for how network hardware transmits data (e.g. cables, radio frequencies, speeds). Standards let equipment from different manufacturers work together.
A set of rules for how data is formatted, addressed and exchanged between devices (e.g. TCP/IP, HTTP).

blocks.text: The standard for wired LANs. Devices connect with cables to a switch, which sends data only to the device it is addressed to.

rows: Common in older installations; maximum 100 m per cable run
Standard for new offices and schools
Maximum 100 m per cable run; better shielding against interference
Used for backbones between buildings and over long distances; immune to electrical interference

blocks.text: Power over Ethernet (PoE) lets one cable carry data and power to devices such as wireless access points, security cameras and VoIP phones, so no power point is needed at the device.
The family of standards for wireless LANs (Wi-Fi). Devices connect using radio waves through a wireless access point (WAP). The "x" stands for the version letter.

blocks.heading: Theoretical vs real speed
blocks.text: Maximum speeds are laboratory figures. Real speeds are much lower because bandwidth is shared between everyone connected to the WAP and drops with distance, walls and interference.

rows: Most congested; affected by microwaves, Bluetooth and neighbouring networks

blocks.text: Wireless networks must be secured with WPA2 or WPA3 encryption and a strong password.

rows: Consistent full speed to each device
Shared between users; varies with distance and obstacles
Affected by interference, walls and congestion
Physical access to a cable or port is needed
Signal travels beyond the building; must be encrypted
Users can move freely within range
Cabling is costly and hard to change once installed
Cheaper and faster to set up; easy to add devices
Up to 100 m per copper cable run
About 30 to 50 m indoors per WAP

blocks.text: Choosing a standard in a LAN design

items: Use Ethernet for fixed devices that need speed and reliability: servers, desktop computers, printers, point-of-sale terminals, security cameras, WAPs (with PoE)
Use wireless for mobile devices and flexible spaces: laptops, tablets, phones, meeting rooms, visitors and guests
Most organisations use both: an Ethernet backbone with WAPs connected by cable to provide wireless coverage

blocks.heading: Exam tip
blocks.text: Always write the standard numbers: 802.3 for Ethernet and 802.11x for wireless. A justification must link a characteristic (speed, reliability, mobility, security, cost) to the needs of the scenario, not just list advantages.

question.text: Compare the Ethernet (802.3) and wireless (802.11x) communication standards.
question.explanation:
4 marks – compares the standards, with two clearly explained similarities or differences
3 marks – compares the standards, with two similarities or differences stated
2 marks – identifies one similarity or difference, or describes each without comparing
1 mark – makes a relevant statement about either standard

Answers could include:
- Both are IEEE standards used to connect devices in a LAN
- 802.3 transmits data through cables, whereas 802.11x uses radio waves, so wireless users can move freely
- 802.3 gives consistent speed and low latency, whereas 802.11x bandwidth is shared and affected by interference
- 802.3 requires physical access to a port, whereas an 802.11x signal extends beyond the building and must be encrypted

question.text: A café is upgrading its network. It needs a connection for its point-of-sale (POS) terminal at the counter, and internet access for customers using their own phones and laptops. Justify the most suitable communication standard for each.
question.explanation:
For each device or user group (x2):
1 mark – identifies a suitable communication standard
3 marks – justifies the choice with detailed reasons linked to the café
2 marks – justifies the choice with limited reasons or links
1 mark – gives one relevant reason
Subtotal 4 marks per group; total 8 marks.

Answers could include:
- POS terminal: Ethernet (802.3). The terminal stays at the counter so it does not need mobility. A cable gives a reliable, low-latency connection so card payments are not interrupted during busy periods, and it cannot be accessed by customers on the wireless network
- Customers: wireless (802.11ax). Customers bring their own phones and laptops, which have no Ethernet ports and move around the café. A separate encrypted guest network gives access without cabling every table and keeps customer traffic away from the POS system

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Explain the purpose of HTTP and HTTPS, and how HTTPS protects data sent between a browser and a web server.

items: Describe the purpose of HTTP
Explain how HTTPS uses a digital certificate and encryption to secure data
Compare HTTP and HTTPS

items.definition: The communication protocol that defines how a browser requests web pages and files from a web server, and how the server responds.
HTTP sent over an encrypted SSL/TLS connection. It encrypts data travelling between the browser and the web server, and uses a digital certificate to verify the server's identity.

items: The user enters a URL or clicks a link
The browser sends an HTTP request to the web server (e.g. GET a page, POST a form)
The server sends back an HTTP response with a status code (e.g. 200 OK, 404 Not Found) and the requested content (HTML, images, CSS)
The browser displays the page

blocks.text: HTTP sends data as plain text. Anyone intercepting the traffic (e.g. on public Wi-Fi) can read or change it.

items: The browser connects to an https:// address
The server sends its digital certificate, which contains the server's public key and is issued by a trusted certificate authority (CA)
The browser checks the certificate is valid, current, issued by a trusted CA and matches the website address
The browser and server use asymmetric encryption (public and private keys) to securely agree on a shared session key
All data for the rest of the session is encrypted with the session key (symmetric encryption)

rows: Plain text; can be read or altered if intercepted
Verified by a digital certificate from a certificate authority
Standard for all websites, essential for logins, payments and personal information

blocks.text: What HTTPS does and does not do

rows: Passwords, payment details and personal information while they travel across the network
Data once it is stored on the server (e.g. if the company is hacked)
Against fake or phishing websites, which can also have HTTPS and a padlock
Against data being altered in transit
Against malware already on the user's device

blocks.heading: Exam tip
blocks.text: Say what is encrypted (data in transit between browser and server) and how (certificate verifies the server, then encryption). "HTTPS is secure" earns no marks. Modern HTTPS uses TLS, the replacement for SSL; the syllabus uses the older name SSL.

question.text: Compare HTTP and HTTPS.
question.explanation:
4 marks – compares HTTP and HTTPS, with two clearly explained similarities or differences
3 marks – compares HTTP and HTTPS, with two similarities or differences stated
2 marks – identifies one similarity or difference, or describes each without comparing
1 mark – makes a relevant statement about HTTP or HTTPS

Answers could include:
- Both are protocols used to transfer web pages between a browser and a web server
- HTTP sends data as plain text, whereas HTTPS encrypts data so it cannot be read if intercepted
- HTTP does not verify the server, whereas HTTPS uses a digital certificate to confirm the server's identity
- HTTP uses port 80, whereas HTTPS uses port 443

question.text: A customer pays for an order on an online store while connected to free café Wi-Fi. Explain how HTTPS protects the customer's payment details.
question.explanation:
3 marks – explains how HTTPS protects the payment details, linked to the scenario
2 marks – describes how HTTPS protects data
1 mark – states that HTTPS encrypts data

Answers could include:
- The store's digital certificate confirms the customer is connected to the genuine store, then the card details are encrypted before leaving the device, so anyone intercepting traffic on the café Wi-Fi sees only unreadable data

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Explain how firewalls, passwords and physical security protect a network, and apply each measure to an organisation's scenario.

items: Describe how a firewall, passwords and physical security each prevent unauthorised access to a network
Explain a network security measure with direct links to a scenario
Identify the limitations of each measure and why organisations use them together

blocks.definition: Hardware, software and physical controls that prevent unauthorised access to a network, its devices and its data, and keep the network available to authorised users.

blocks.text: The syllabus names three types: firewalls, passwords and physical security.

blocks.definition: Hardware or software that monitors incoming and outgoing network traffic and allows or blocks each data packet based on a set of security rules. It creates a barrier between a trusted internal network (the LAN) and an untrusted external network (the internet).

rows: A separate device, or built into the router, between the internet connection and the switch
A firewall appliance at a business connecting its office LAN to the NBN
That one device, including when it is used away from the office on public Wi-Fi
Windows Defender Firewall on a staff laptop

blocks.definition: A secret string of characters that authenticates a user, so only authorised people can log in to the network, devices, Wi-Fi and online services, with access set by their user account.

rows: Every user has an individual account and password, never a shared one
Access can be limited by role, and audit trails show exactly who did what
Long passphrases, e.g. four or more random words (at least 14 characters)
Length makes passwords much harder to guess or crack by brute force
A unique password for every system
One stolen password does not unlock other accounts
Multi-factor authentication (MFA), e.g. a code on an authenticator app
A stolen password alone is not enough to log in
Account lockout after several failed attempts
Change default passwords on routers, WAPs and printers
Default passwords are published online and easy to find
Secure the Wi-Fi with WPA2 or WPA3 and a strong network key
Stops people within range joining the network
Disable accounts as soon as staff leave

blocks.definition: Physical controls that stop unauthorised people reaching, tampering with, damaging or stealing network hardware such as servers, switches, routers, WAPs and storage devices.

rows: Locked server room or locked network cabinet (rack)
The server, switch and router are kept in a locked room, not under the reception desk
Keycard or biometric (fingerprint) access to the server room, recording who entered and when
CCTV covering the server room and entrances
Unused Ethernet wall ports disabled; WAPs mounted on the ceiling out of reach
Cable locks for desktop computers; laptops locked away after hours
Uninterruptible power supply (UPS), fire suppression and air conditioning in the server room, so the network stays available
Fencing, security guards and reinforced walls at the provider's data centre
Unauthorised traffic entering or leaving the network from outside
Someone walking into the server room and taking the server
Unauthorised users logging in to devices, accounts and Wi-Fi
Attacks that do not need a login, e.g. unrequested traffic from the internet
Theft, damage or tampering with network hardware
A hacker accessing the network remotely

blocks.text: No single measure is enough. Each covers a gap left by the others, so organisations use all three as layers of protection.

question.text: Describe two network security measures that protect a network from unauthorised access.
question.explanation:
For each security measure (x2):
2 marks – describes how the security measure protects the network
1 mark – makes a general comment about the security measure
Subtotal 2 marks per measure; total 4 marks.

Answers could include:
- Firewall: inspects each packet entering or leaving the network and blocks any that do not meet its rules, preventing unauthorised access from the internet
- Passwords: users must enter the correct password before accessing the network, so only authorised users can use its devices and data
- Physical security: servers and network devices are kept in a locked room, so unauthorised people cannot tamper with, damage or steal them

question.text: A real estate agency has 12 staff in one office. The file server sits under the reception desk, where customers wait. All staff log in with the same username and password. The NBN modem router connects directly to the office switch, and customers are given the office Wi-Fi password so they can use their phones. Explain three network security measures the agency should use to protect its network.
question.explanation:
For each network security measure (x3):
3 marks – explains the network security measure in direct reference to the scenario
2 marks – makes general comments about the network security measure
1 mark – identifies an aspect of the network security measure
Subtotal 3 marks per measure; total 9 marks.

Answers could include:
- Firewall: the modem router connects straight to the switch with no firewall. A hardware firewall between the NBN connection and the switch would inspect incoming traffic and block unauthorised connections, and a separate guest network would stop customers' phones reaching the file server
- Passwords: all staff share one login, so the agency cannot control or trace who accesses client files. Each staff member should have an individual account with a long, unique password and MFA, and customers should use a separate guest Wi-Fi password so the office network key is not given out
- Physical security: the server is under the reception desk where customers wait, so it could be stolen, unplugged or tampered with. It should be moved into a locked room or network cabinet with keycard access, so only authorised staff can reach it

blocks.heading: Revision
blocks.text: Revise the Networks topic: communication protocols (TCP/IP, HTTP/HTTPS), communication standards (802.3 Ethernet and 802.11x wireless), network security measures (firewalls, passwords, physical security), and designing and justifying a LAN.

topics.title: Impacts of Technology
topics.description: Covers the security of personal and sensitive data, workplace codes of conduct, issues with cloud computing, online censorship in a global context, and the impact of digital technologies, global markets and Web 2.0/Web 3.0 on organisations and individuals.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Explain the four issues with the use of cloud computing and link each issue to an organisation's situation.

items: Describe the four issues: confidentiality of data, sensitivity of documents, level of accessibility and availability of online applications
Suggest a strategy that reduces each issue
Explain an issue with direct links to a scenario

blocks.definition: Storing data and running applications on servers owned by a third-party provider and accessed over the internet, instead of on the organisation's own computers (e.g. Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, AWS).

rows: Keeping data private so only authorised people can read it
The organisation no longer has full control of its data. The provider's staff, hackers or a breach at the provider could expose it.
Encrypt data (with the organisation holding the keys), choose a provider with strong security certifications, check the SLA and privacy policy
Some documents cause serious harm if released (health records, legal files, financial or commercial plans)
Sensitive files may be misplaced, shared publicly by mistake, or stored in countries with weaker privacy laws
Classify documents by sensitivity, keep the most sensitive data in Australian data centres or on-premises, follow Privacy Act 1988 obligations
Who can access which data, and what they can do with it (view, edit, delete)
If every user can access everything, staff may view or change data they should not see
Set access privileges by role, use multi-factor authentication, review permissions regularly, keep audit trails
Whether cloud applications and data can be used when they are needed
Work stops during internet outages or provider downtime; the provider may change prices, remove features or close the service
Choose a provider with an uptime guarantee in the SLA, have a backup internet connection, keep offline copies of critical files, plan for moving to another provider

blocks.text: Benefits to weigh against the issues

items: Access from any location and device, supporting remote work
Real-time collaboration on shared files
No need to buy and maintain servers; costs scale with use
The provider handles updates, backups and security patches

blocks.text: Example: a hospital moves patient records to the cloud

rows: Patient records held by a third party could be exposed if the provider is hacked, so the hospital must check the provider's encryption and security safeguards
Medical records are sensitive information under the Privacy Act; a leak could cause patients serious harm and lead to legal action
Reception staff need appointment details but not full medical histories, so access must be restricted by role
If the cloud system is down, doctors cannot view patient histories during treatment, so the SLA must guarantee high uptime and there must be a backup plan

question.text: Explain two issues a business might face in using cloud computing.
question.explanation: Marking key: for each issue (x2), explains an issue a business may face with the use of cloud computing (3 marks), describes an issue (2 marks), or makes a superficial comment about an issue (1 mark). Total 6.

question.text: A physiotherapy clinic with three locations plans to move its patient records and booking system to a cloud service. With reference to the scenario, explain the following issues: confidentiality of data, level of accessibility, availability of online applications.
question.explanation:
Marking key: for each issue (x3), explains the issue making direct links to the scenario (3 marks), describes the issue making direct links to the scenario (2 marks), or makes general comments about the issue (1 mark). Total 9.

Answers could include:
- Confidentiality of data: the clinic's patient records will be stored on a third party's servers, so the clinic loses direct control. It must check that the provider encrypts the data and has strong safeguards, or a breach could expose patients' health information
- Level of accessibility: staff at all three locations will log in to the same system, so access must be set by role. Physiotherapists need treatment notes, while reception staff only need bookings and contact details
- Availability of online applications: if the internet connection at one location fails or the provider has an outage, staff cannot see bookings or treatment notes. The clinic should choose a provider with a high uptime guarantee in its SLA and keep a backup connection

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand the purpose of a Code of Conduct and how it regulates employee behaviour, particularly regarding ICT systems.

items: Define the purpose of a Code of Conduct in a workplace
Describe five key elements of a Code of Conduct related to ICT use
Explain employer monitoring rights and employee responsibilities

blocks.definition: A formal written document that outlines expected standards of behaviour for employees. It establishes clear rules about workplace conduct, particularly around ICT system use. Breaches can result in disciplinary action, including suspension or termination.

blocks.text: Elements of a code of conduct include:

items: Work hours
Employee email use
Employee internet use
Employee privacy
Employer's monitoring of work emails, internet access and computer use

blocks.text: Codes of Conduct establish boundaries around when work communication is expected.

items: Defines standard work hours and expectations for availability
Clarifies whether employees must respond to emails or messages outside work hours
Specifies emergency situations that may require out-of-hours contact
Protects employee wellbeing by preventing constant connectivity demands

blocks.text: Example: A retail business code specifies that employees should not access work email after 6 pm unless managing an emergency.
Under Australia's Fair Work Act 2009, employees can refuse to monitor, read or respond to work-related contact outside their working hours, unless that refusal would be unreasonable.
This should be considered in workplace codes of conduct, particularly rules covering work hours, email and digital communication.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective

items: Describe online censorship, including who carries it out and how

blocks.definition: The control of what can be accessed, published or viewed on the internet. It can be carried out by governments, regulators, private organisations (platforms, schools, workplaces) or by individuals themselves (self-censorship). It includes filtering and blocking content, removing it, and monitoring or penalising users who access or publish certain content.

rows: Block websites and apps; filter keywords; order content removal; shut down the internet
China's "Great Firewall" blocks Google, Facebook and many news sites
Issue legal notices requiring platforms to remove content
Australia's eSafety Commissioner orders removal of cyber abuse material
Content moderation rules; remove posts; suspend accounts; limit reach of posts
YouTube removes videos that breach its community guidelines
Web filters block categories of websites on their network
Schools block gambling and adult sites; workplaces block social media
Self-censorship: avoiding posting views for fear of consequences
Users in some countries avoid criticising the government online

blocks.text: Online censorship in a global context

rows: The "Great Firewall" blocks foreign platforms and news sites, and filters keywords about politically sensitive topics. Local platforms must remove banned content.
Blocks independent news sites and restricts foreign social media platforms, especially during conflict
Governments have shut down or slowed the internet during protests and elections to stop people organising and sharing information
The Digital Services Act requires large platforms to remove illegal content quickly and explain how they moderate content

Targeted removal of harmful and illegal content by a regulator, plus age restrictions on social media (see below). Political opinion is not systematically blocked, but regulation of online content is increasing and debated.

Gives the eSafety Commissioner power to order the removal of cyberbullying of children, adult cyber abuse, image-based abuse (sharing intimate images without consent) and illegal or restricted content such as child abuse and terrorist material. Platforms that fail to comply can be fined.
Australia's independent online safety regulator. Handles complaints, issues removal notices and enforces industry codes.

Age-restricted platforms such as TikTok, Instagram, Snapchat, Facebook, YouTube and X must take reasonable steps to stop Australians under 16 having accounts. The responsibility and fines (up to $49.5 million) fall on platforms, not children or parents. Messaging, online gaming, education and health services are exempt.
Since 2015, copyright owners can apply to the Federal Court to make internet service providers block overseas piracy websites

blocks.text: Case study: eSafety vs X (2024). After a stabbing at a Sydney church in April 2024, the eSafety Commissioner ordered X to remove video of the attack. X blocked the posts for Australian users but refused to remove them worldwide. The Federal Court did not extend an order forcing global removal, and eSafety later dropped the case. This shows the global problem: a national regulator has limited power over content hosted by an overseas company for users in other countries.

items: Protect citizens from harmful content (terrorism, child abuse material, hate speech)
Protect children (age restrictions, cyberbullying removal)
Reduce crime such as piracy, scams and illegal gambling
Protect national security
Maintain political stability or control, including hiding information that damages the government's reputation
Enforce cultural, religious or social values

rows: Reduces exposure to harmful, violent or illegal content

Protects children and vulnerable users from abuse and exploitation
Governments can manipulate what citizens see to sway opinion or hide wrongdoing
Gives victims a faster way to have abusive content removed than going to court

Increases workplace productivity when distracting sites are blocked

Age checks may require users to hand over personal data, raising privacy concerns

Demonstrate depth: Shows consideration for the practical realities of development (e.g., performance, accessibility, maintenance).
Guide decisions: Provides a clear, logical rationale for the design and technical features selected for the final project.
Be specific: Avoid generic statements. Instead of "it is hard to make," use "requires complex API integration which increases development time."
Be realistic: A high-quality PMI identifies genuine challenges; do not ignore the minuses.
Think user-first: Always evaluate how these choices impact the end-user experience and accessibility.

question.text: Which of the following is a principle of design rather than an element of design?
question.explanation: Unity is a principle (a rule for arranging elements, achieved through proximity and repetition). Texture, line and colour are all elements — the building blocks themselves, not the rules for arranging them.

question.text: A laptop loses everything stored in RAM the moment it loses power, but keeps everything on its SSD. This is because RAM is:
question.explanation: Volatile memory loses its contents when power is removed — this is RAM. Non-volatile memory and storage (like an SSD) keeps its contents without power.

question.text: A photographer's work is automatically protected in Australia the moment it is taken, with no registration required, for their lifetime plus 70 years. Which form of intellectual property protection is this?
question.explanation: Copyright under the Copyright Act 1968 protects the original expression of an idea automatically once it is recorded — no registration needed, lasting the creator's life plus 70 years. Patents, trade marks and registered designs all require formal registration.

question.text: A regional business lets staff attend meetings from home using live video calls. This is an example of which form of collaboration?
question.explanation: Synchronous collaboration is real-time communication with immediate responses — live video meetings and voice calls. Asynchronous collaboration (email, discussion boards) has a time delay between responses.

question.text: A small business chooses Google Workspace over buying licensed desktop software, specifically so the team always has the latest version without installing anything. Which advantage of online software does this describe?
question.explanation: Automatic updates means online software updates itself, so users always have the latest features and security fixes without manually installing anything, and don't have to wait to install software upfront.

question.text: A UX designer organises a website so related content is grouped together and the most important content appears first. This is best described as:
question.explanation: Logical and hierarchical structure means related content is grouped together, with the most important content first — part of how a digital product's structure is organised so users can find information and move through it easily.

question.text: A business lets customers submit support requests through a web page, and the responses are stored centrally for the support team to review. The web page is best described as:
question.explanation: An online form is a web-based document that collects structured data from users and stores the responses in a central location for analysis — exactly this use case. A CMS is for publishing content, not collecting it.

question.text: Which protocol encrypts the data travelling between a browser and a web server, and uses a digital certificate to verify the server's identity?
question.explanation: HTTPS is HTTP sent over an encrypted SSL/TLS connection — it encrypts the data in transit and uses a digital certificate to verify the server's identity. HTTP alone does not encrypt anything.

question.text: A streaming platform's recommendation engine personalises content for each user and runs partly on blockchain-based ownership of digital assets. This reflects a shift toward:
question.explanation: Web 3.0 is the intelligent, decentralised web — AI personalises content, and blockchain lets users own their data and digital assets. Web 2.0 is the earlier read-write social web (users create and share content, but without this AI/blockchain layer).

question.text: A company contracts an external provider to manage its data backups and sets a written agreement specifying the provider's required uptime and what happens if it isn't met. This written agreement is a:
question.explanation: A service level agreement (SLA) is a written agreement between a provider and a client setting out the services to be delivered, the standard each must meet, and the consequence if that standard isn't met.
